items.description: arXiv:2610.16288v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback--response cycles elicited by replay in the target model. Our training-free framework, $\textbf{REVEAL}$ ($\textbf{REV}$erse $\textbf{E}$ngineering $\textbf{A}$gentic $\textbf{L}$atents), uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match and select local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task and source model. Their response-transition contrasts yield a target-specific steering direction, applied before each response. Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy than unmodified agents across three targets. Representation analyses and behavioral case studies support reusing frontier-model experience as local activation control.

items.title: Memory-Efficient Integer-Only Training of Deep Neural Networks
items.description: arXiv:2610.16298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training neural networks in reduced precision can yield significant efficiency gains, yet all existing methods that scale to standard computer vision benchmarks retain floating-point in at least one stage, typically the weight update or optimizer state. We present a training algorithm that scales to modern deep neural networks, in which every tensor (weights, gradients, and activations) is stored as INT8, and every operation (forward pass, backward pass, weight update, optimizer update) is performed in integer arithmetic. Specifically, tensors are stored as signed integer mantissas paired with explicit power-of-two exponents, on which integer-only operations are performed using five custom composable building blocks (products, sums, divide-by-constant, nonlinear functions, and weight updates). This allows complete implementation of trainable integer layers, including convolutions, batch and layer normalization, softmax, and GELU. A per-group velocity mechanism with independent exponent tracking preserves gradient precision across neurons and channels with diverse magnitudes. As every tensor fits in INT8, training memory is roughly 4x smaller than the FP32 baseline. We validate our training algorithm on CNNs (ResNet-18/34/50/101, MobileNetV2) and Vision Transformers (ViT-Ti / B), demonstrating for the first time that training neural networks with INT8 tensors and integer arithmetic can achieve competitive accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet at a reduced memory budget.

items.title: FON: A Draft-Revise Dual-Organ Language Model without Sequence-Level Quadratic Attention
items.description: arXiv:2610.16301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-attention assigns two functions to one mechanism-where to read and how to mix-at the price of O(L^2) training, an O(T) decode state, and position signals bound to the training length. Existing attention-free alternatives all optimize the single function of generation. We propose FON (Fusion-Organ Network), which differentiates one weight stack into a drafting organ (multi-tap learnable delays + content-adaptive recursion; causal, O(S) training, O(1) decode state, no sequence-level quadratic attention) and a revision organ that re-processes the written prefix through multi-scale ripple kernels injected via weak gates, never generating. At 30M parameters, iso-parameter and iso-token budget, FON reaches perplexity 131.03 on WikiText-103, beating Transformer (197.73) and Mamba2 (152.53); the advantage persists under all depth-aligned baselines and at the 70M tier (-20.8%). At 8x length extrapolation FON degrades by ~8-9% without positional-encoding engineering, between ALiBi and RoPE. The revision channel provides a structural pathway for in-domain infilling that causal architectures lack in principle (+19% over on-demand coupling), at a perplexity cost indistinguishable within measurement precision. We report all costs and boundaries: impaired long-range retrieval, synthetic-task disadvantages, weaker out-of-domain code infilling than a same-recipe Transformer, and a 6.5-12.3x wall-clock gap.

items.title: Narrative Paradoxes in LLM Inference: Shaping Reasoning Trajectories toward Misalignment
items.description: arXiv:2610.16312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explicit reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often associated with reliability, yet it can still pose risks when a model infers harmful goals under a benign context. We identify a distinct challenge: ensuring the safety of the \emph{multi-step reasoning process} itself, where locally coherent steps may still lead to globally harmful outcomes. To explore this vulnerability, we propose PDRA (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack), a novel attack method that programs a harmful reasoning trajectory. PDRA first constructs a paradoxical narrative core by pairing a malicious actor (e.g., a terrorist) with a benign task (e.g., writing a safety bulletin). It then embeds this core into a structured analytical framework that forces the model through a mandatory three-stage analysis -- surface purpose, latent intent, and operational reconstruction -- guiding it to produce detailed harmful content while maintaining narrative coherence. Mechanistically, we show PDRA steers the model's internal representations away from refusal-related patterns, suppressing safety-triggering lexicons while activating planning-oriented terms. Empirically, PDRA achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse LLMs with high efficiency. \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Warning:} This paper may contain sensitive content.}

items.title: ReTAC: Residual Test-Time Agentic Computation for Video Spatial Reasoning
items.description: arXiv:2610.16315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.

items.title: HyWe: Unifying Search and Operation for Real-World Hybrid Web Tasks
items.description: arXiv:2610.16319v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world hybrid web tasks need both information gathering and page interaction, yet search-based and operation-based agents are developed and evaluated separately. To bridge this gap, we introduce HyWe, a framework that unifies both capabilities within one model and trajectory. Its two modes use dedicated prompts and tool sets to sustain sub-goal execution; explicit switching selects the needed capability, and shared history lets each mode build on the other's findings. To provide demonstrations of these behaviors, we develop HyWeCollector, a fully automatic pipeline that uses task prototypes, four switching patterns, and multi-agent synthesis to produce verified hybrid trajectories. We train HyWe-35B on these demonstrations to unify efficient information gathering and browser interaction in a single 35B web agent. To evaluate hybrid task completion, we introduce HyWeBench: 100 human-written tasks on websites distinct from training, with human-written sub-goal checklists and an outcome-based evaluation pipeline. Hybrid training enables HyWe-35B to achieve 47.0% success on this benchmark, improving on the untrained base model by 19.0 percentage points and outperforming existing search-based and operation-based agents. Even before training, the same base model solves 28.0% of tasks with HyWe, versus 11.0% with all tools under one prompt. Beyond hybrid tasks, HyWe-35B achieves 59.0% and 88.3% success on Online-Mind2Web and WebVoyager, outperforming existing open-source baselines and cutting action cost per successful task by 48.3% and 51.9% compared with Fara-7B.

items.title: When a Conceptor Complement Becomes Gain: Operator Geometry and Behavioral Attribution in Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.16325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a steering intervention changes a language model's behavior, which part of the intervention deserves the credit? We test this question for a target-centered, scaled conceptor complement by removing its fitted covariance filter while preserving the same target-specific center and gain. At the original aperture $\alpha=.05$ and gain $\beta=2$, all 21 fitted maps across three models and seven targets expand every direction at the generation intervention layers. The matrix correction is $0.093\%$--$7.815\%$ of the matched-control displacement on held-out extraction activations. In 480 paired comparisons within a 1,920-response study, retaining the matrix changes many individual texts but does not establish a consistent additional target-suppression benefit on the four-target panel. A geometric aperture sweep shows that the operating regime changes with the filter setting. Separately, an invertible soft filter preserves what an unrestricted affine readout can recover, whereas dedicated erasure methods reduce prediction by newly fitted probes. Together, the results show why a whole-intervention comparison cannot by itself attribute generated behavior to the fitted matrix: analyze the complete transformation, hold shared components fixed, and test its output consequences directly.

items.title: TRAP: Tool-result Replay Attack for Probing Misbinding in LLM Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.16333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI agents increasingly act through external tools, tool results are no longer simple outputs but execution artifacts that must remain correctly associated with the context that produced them. Yet as results persist across caches, recovery mechanisms, and shared runtime state, this association can break, causing a real and unmodified result to be consumed in an incompatible execution context and lead the agent to an unsafe action. We characterize this failure as tool-result misbinding. To systematically study this failure, we introduce ReplayBench, a benchmark that uses controlled tool-result replay to evaluate misbinding across 19 representative agent scenarios, 4 failure properties, and 3 replay mechanisms. Across eight LLMs, three agent frameworks, and diverse stateful workflows, we find widespread replay-induced failures, with a mean Final-State Error Rate of 0.649 under cross-task replay. Stage-wise analysis localizes these failures to model-side action generation. Further analyses show that replay susceptibility varies with task similarity, shows little dependence on object similarity, and remains high under result staleness and implicit environment changes. These findings motivate runtime validity mechanisms that eliminate final-state errors in our evaluated settings while preserving legitimate recovery. The results call for explicit contextual binding in tool-using agent runtimes. Our work is public at https://github.com/Phitooo/Replaybench.

items.title: Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning via Confidence-Guided Adaptive Debate
items.description: arXiv:2610.16343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent debate has shown promise for improving the reasoning of large language models, yet recent theory suggests its benefits are highly regime-dependent. While interaction can amplify informative signals under corrective conditions, symmetric debate dynamics are neutral in expectation, often making majority voting preferable. We reconcile these views by arguing that debate is effective only when invoked at the right time and with appropriate structure. Based on this insight, we propose LASE: Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement, a leader-centric multi-agent debate framework that selectively engages interaction only in non-neutral regimes. LASE introduces an asymmetric leader-supporter architecture that enables directed information flow and selective signal amplification, while defaulting to simple aggregation otherwise. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks show that LASE achieves multi-agent-level performance with near single-agent token cost, substantially improving efficiency over static debate and voting baselines.

items.title: ChronoScribe: Semantic-Numerical Specialization for Instruction-Driven Time Series Forecasting
items.description: arXiv:2610.16345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in instruction-driven time series forecasting highlight a fundamental tension: systems must simultaneously master natural-language instruction following and precise numerical prediction. Current approaches often force a compromise. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret unstructured requests but may be inaccurate when asked to produce forecast values directly, whereas time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide numerical forecasts but typically require structured inputs specifying the target series, context window, and horizon. We present ChronoScribe, which applies semantic-numerical specialization to this workflow. A LoRA-adapted LLM proposes an execution path and context length; deterministic rules resolve the executable configuration. On the specialist path, a frozen TSFM produces quantile trajectories for the task-specified horizon. Deterministic trajectory summaries condition the response, while the LLM neither generates nor revises predicted values. We evaluate a Qwen3.5-9B--Chronos-2 implementation across 23 evaluation dimensions and 30 public datasets against eleven proprietary direct LLMs and three open TSFMs. ChronoScribe has the lowest error on sMAPE, MASE, WAPE, RMSE, and MAE among all evaluated systems, including fixed-context controls. Across these metrics, even the lowest direct-LLM error remains 2.0--2.7 times the corresponding ChronoScribe error. At the system level, ChronoScribe achieves a Task-Level Score (TLS) of 65.5, 10.6 points above the strongest direct-LLM baseline. The results support ChronoScribe's division of labor, in which the LLM handles interpretation, configuration, and communication while the TSFM handles numerical forecasting.

items.title: World Models Need a Physical Registry: Learning Internal Predictive States for Physically Plausible World Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.16365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video world models must generate physically plausible futures, not just realistic frames. Existing approaches typically use semantic, physical, or predictive information to guide the visual generation stream, leaving a fundamental question: where inside the generator should predictions of scene evolution live? Standard video tokens jointly encode appearance and dynamics, but provide no distinct state for learning and reading predictive dynamics. We answer this question with the Physical Registry: temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with video tokens, and receive future-representation supervision, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. In a controlled comparison of predictive-state interfaces on Physics-IQ Verified, Physical Registry improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9/8.7 points on I2V/V2V, the largest gain among the interfaces we compare. Across all Cosmos and WAN backbones, Physical Registry improves Physics-IQ Verified scores. With only 0.45% additional parameters, it enables Cosmos 3 Nano 16B to surpass the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B (43.56 vs. 42.7). On WorldModelBench, it also improves physical adherence and the total score for all four evaluated backbones. Because the registry becomes candidate-specific while remaining readable, the Physical Registry Selector (PRS) ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate registry readouts depart from the shared forecast before full denoising is complete. Across four backbones, this selection improves I2V scores by 5.6-15.9% without completed-video external scoring. Together, these results support a broader principle: dynamics prediction should live as an explicit model state that co-evolves with the video representation. Project page: https://grainsack.github.io/physical-registry/

items.title: RetroPlanner: Multi-Route Expansion and Multi-Objective Reasoning for LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning
items.description: arXiv:2610.16391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is often considered solved once a route to purchasable starting materials is found, but such a route should also be practical in real-world chemistry. Recent LLM-based planners formulate this process as sequential decision-making over an AND-OR graph, yet typically expand a single molecule per turn and are optimized for solvability alone, leaving alternative routes uncompared across the multiple objectives that determine practicality before the search budget is committed. We introduce RetroPlanner, an LLM-based planner that jointly compares multiple routes to steer the search toward higher synthesizability, as measured by reaction plausibility, round-trip consistency, and starting-material price. RetroPlanner is trained to reason over chemical evidence: structural progress from the target molecule, bond changes and reaction classes, where candidate routes diverge from one another, and how they rank across multiple objectives. Experiments on multi-step retrosynthesis benchmarks demonstrate that RetroPlanner recovers more alternative routes than prior LLM-based planners while improving synthetic route quality and maintaining a high success rate.

items.title: Recursive Environment Scaling for General Long-Horizon Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.16397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study environment scaling as a way to increase agent-benchmark difficulty while holding core task objectives fixed. Our framework, Recursive Environment Scaling (RES), transforms existing benchmark environments while preserving their objectives and completion requirements. A proposer changes information access, resource relations, and execution dependencies; execution-grounded checks validate the resulting candidate, and accepted changes are inherited across rounds. This produces related environments for paired evaluation and training-trajectory collection. Experiments on 294 initial tasks from three benchmarks show lower task success for all six evaluation models, with decreases of 57.14--77.14 percentage points on Claw-Eval-Live. With equal trajectory counts and identical optimization settings, fine-tuning on RES trajectories outperforms original-trajectory SFT in all nine model--benchmark comparisons by 7.00--14.61 percentage points. Ablations identify recursive inheritance and dependency composition as important contributors to increased difficulty. Together, these results support environment scaling for both agent evaluation and training.

items.title: EvoWeb: A Benchmark for Coding Agents on Evolving Web Applications
items.description: arXiv:2610.16402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web application development often proceeds through successive requests that extend an existing implementation. Yet web-generation benchmarks primarily evaluate development toward fixed specifications. We introduce EvoWeb, a novel benchmark comprising 320 cumulative requests over 32 web applications, grounded in real-world product features and structured by functional dependency graphs. Agents iteratively modify a persistent codebase, while a multimodal web agent tests each intermediate application in a live browser, assessing newly requested functionality, cross-request integration, and previously requested functionality. To characterize reliability throughout development, we integrate trajectory performance across user-tolerance thresholds rather than impose a fixed stopping criterion. Experiments across open- and closed-source frontier models show that EvoWeb reveals clear performance differences between models, with cross-request integration emerging as a key challenge. Further analysis shows that later requests with deeper or more numerous dependencies are solved less accurately, while runtime errors become more frequent over successive requests. EvoWeb provides a testbed for evaluating and improving coding agents in long-horizon, multi-request development.

items.title: SLS-Bench: A Benchmark for Incident Log Summarization with Synthetic Observability Data
items.description: arXiv:2610.16412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As IT systems grow in complexity, automated agent-driven incident response becomes increasingly critical. A key capability for these agents is summarizing large log streams into human-readable reports. Further progress requires meaningfully evaluating this function, yet existing benchmarks leave end-to-end summarization from large log streams underexplored due to the prohibitive cost and complexity of collecting real-world data. We introduce SLS-Bench, a benchmark for incident log summarization featuring 90 tasks grounded in real-world incident reports, each with a synthetic log stream and a reference summary. To construct SLS-Bench, we developed a data generation pipeline that converts incident reports into structured incident models, which guide the generation of synthetic logs and reference summaries. This pipeline combines narrative grounding, explicit incident modeling, generator-verifier loops, and statistical comparisons with real-world log streams to produce realistic and controllable observability data. Our evaluation of 14 LLMs on SLS-Bench shows that while frontier models can produce useful summaries, they do so at substantial cost and latency, and open-weight models lag significantly. SLS-Bench provides a framework for systematic evaluation of log analysis agents and a scalable blueprint for future synthetic observability benchmarks.

items.title: Chain Dimension Scaling: Communication-Efficient Loop-Style Scaling for Industrial Short-Video Ranking
items.description: arXiv:2610.16415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial recommendation rankers keep scaling in width and depth to billions of parameters, but this increasingly incurs costs in parameter growth, distributed communication overhead, and training inefficiency. We introduce \underline{C}hain \underline{D}imension \underline{S}caling (CDS), a scaling strategy orthogonal to width and depth. CDS repeatedly applies a single feature-interaction block with parameters shared across iterations, so the number of iterations (the chain length) becomes a new scaling dimension that adds no parameters. A lightweight intra-chain residual connection stabilizes optimization and improves quality. CDS enables two regimes. In the \emph{compression regime}, shallow blocks with a longer chain match deeper baselines with fewer parameters and faster training; in the \emph{quality-scaling regime}, increasing chain length under a fixed parameter budget yields consistent offline and online gains, suggesting the chain dimension adds modeling capacity beyond parameter reuse. We evaluate CDS in a large-scale multi-task short-video ranking system in production. In the compression regime, CDS stays within $0.03\%$ of baseline offline quality while reducing trainable parameters by 26.6\% and improving training throughput by 6.4\%, with neutral-to-positive online participation. In the quality-scaling regime, quality improves monotonically with chain length. Wall-clock analysis shows the efficiency gain comes mainly not from reduced FLOPs but from lower cross-device synchronization overhead and reduced optimizer update cost. These results position parameter-shared iterative computation as a practical, communication-efficient scaling axis for industrial ranking systems.

items.title: AuthGateBench: Benchmarking LLMs as Authorization Gate
items.description: arXiv:2610.16426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated approval systems let coding agents execute high-risk actions with minimal human oversight by delegating the authorization decision to a classifier, typically a large language model (LLM). Such systems, adopted in tools like Claude Code and Codex, remain vulnerable to failure modes such as scope escalation, where the agent takes actions exceeding what the user authorized. Existing benchmarks focus mainly on malicious requests, evaluating refusal under an implicit policy. We introduce AuthGateBench, the first policy-guided benchmark for authorization gating under benign requests. We implement a novel pipeline where an LLM generates contrast pairs with identical action and trajectory but differing request, flipping the label between block and allow. This allows us to assess whether models reason over context rather than the action alone. We further examine whether auxiliary environment signals can help models make better decisions. The resulting benchmark comprises 1,400 instances spanning five failure modes drawn from real-world Claude Code incidents. Evaluations show accuracy degrades unevenly across failure modes as models over-rely on internal safety alignment, and models still block most actions even when explicitly authorized, revealing unstable rather than deterministic decisions; retrospectively retrieved environment signals, however, substantially improve authorization accuracy.

items.title: RAP-WAM: Learning World-Action Models through Predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations
items.description: arXiv:2610.16443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent world action models draw on video generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Adapting these priors to control requires determining how future predictions should guide policy learning. RAP-WAM combines predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations (RAP) with future-supervised queries and Coupled Action Projection for policy learning. Predictive rehearsal trains on model-generated inputs while retaining recorded targets, and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior. We perturb actions and measure changes in video predictions. Action-response-based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision; spatially aggregating the responses determines supervision intensity across future action steps. No separate scoring network or deployment-time probe is required. The base learns from a video-pretrained backbone without intermediate pretraining on external embodied data. We evaluate the fixed base and its agent-refined, task-conditioned system. On 42 RoboDojo tasks, their average success rates are 12.85% and 15.62%, with Scores of 17.86 and 20.59. Across 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieves 89.00% task-macro-average success, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 37.67 percentage points. Across 315 fixed-output simulation windows, 45.21% of response-top20 positions fall outside error-top20, revealing information beyond prediction error.

items.title: XAI-Guided Fourier Domain Generalisation for Pure-Simulation Sim-to-Real Deep Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.16478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for vision-based autonomous driving, but policies trained in simulation often suffer severe performance degradation when deployed in the real world. Existing sim-to-real methods commonly address this gap through image-transfer-based domain adaptation or policy-agnostic domain randomisation. However, the former requires laborious acquisition of target-domain data and is often limited to the deployment domain, whereas the latter introduces unguided perturbations that may not reflect the underlying sim-to-real discrepancy, leading to suboptimal transfer performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose XFD, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-guided Fourier domain generalisation framework for pure-simulation sim-to-real reinforcement learning. The proposed framework extracts explainability attribution maps from simulated observations, and converts these attributions into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain interventions. By perturbing appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structures, XFD constructs robustness-enhancing visual domains entirely within simulation. Subsequently, the proposed robust policy optimisation guides the policy towards attending to task-critical features while suppressing sensitivity to irrelevant visual information. Extensive experiments in simulation and zero-shot real-world deployment demonstrate that XFD consistently improves traveled distance and reward over standard policy and randomly domain-randomised baseline, especially on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds. Attribution-based analysis further proves that the proposed policy preserves more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and real-world observations.

items.title: PXRD-Bench: How Close Are We to Determining Crystal Structures from Powder Diffraction?
items.description: arXiv:2610.16480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) would enable routine characterization of newly synthesized materials, including those absent from reference databases. Generative models offer a promising approach, but existing evaluations remain fragmented and largely assume single-phase samples with known composition. To fill this gap, we introduce PXRD-Bench, a unified benchmark that extends evaluation to unknown per-element atom counts and recovery of both structures in two-phase mixtures. It provides approximately 4.1 million training structures with simulated PXRD, tests generalization to unseen compositions and structural prototypes, and evaluates recovery from experimental PXRD after excluding structurally matching training entries. To provide a strong reference baseline, we also introduce Bragglite, a PXRD-to-structure model developed through a systematic study of PXRD modeling choices. It achieves a 44.2\% Top-1 match rate on experimental RRUFF patterns with known composition, 24.6\% above the strongest prior baseline. Further analysis yields several key findings: some models fail to benefit from experimental PXRD, while generalization to unseen structural prototypes and recovery from two-phase mixtures remain challenging. Together, our benchmark, systematic studies, and Bragglite clarify the capabilities and limitations of current PXRD-to-structure models.

items.title: Boosting the Learning for Ranking Patterns
items.description: arXiv:2610.16511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pattern mining is a valuable tool for exploratory data analysis, but identifying relevant patterns for a specific user is challenging. Various interestingness mea- sures have been developed to evaluate patterns, but they may not efficiently estimate user-specific functions. Learning user-specific functions by ranking patterns has been proposed, but this requires significant time and training samples. In this paper, we present a solution that formulates the problem of learning pattern ranking functions as a multicriteria decision making problem. Our approach uses Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) to elicit weights for different interestingness measures based on user preference. We also propose an active learning mode with a sensitivity-based heuristic to minimize user ranking queries while still providing high-quality results. Experiments show that our approach significantly reduces running time and returns precise pattern ranking while being robust to user error, compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

items.title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents
items.description: arXiv:2610.16523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.

items.title: Does the Explanation Drift Before the Guarantee? Label-Free Early Warning on Evolving Graphs
items.description: arXiv:2610.16534v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed models can fail silently as the world they describe evolves. Attribution drift has served as an early warning in tabular data; we ask whether, in graph streams, a model's own explanations can forewarn the loss of nominal conformal coverage. Doing so requires repairing the naive drift statistic twice. A vanishing edge loses mask mass regardless of whether the model relied on it, so we condition the importance on edge presence. Evolving graphs also break edge identity: a relabelling that changes nothing shifts the identity-based statistic by 0.69 on synthetic graphs and 0.83 on real ego-networks, whereas aggregating over structural roles brings both to 0.0 and stays well-defined when the support changes. We test six pre-registered regimes on thirty seeds each. A two-channel monitor, tracking conditional mask mass and its distribution over roles, precedes coverage collapse by 8 to 14.5 steps across four gradual regimes (node addition, removal, replacement, and edge thinning), all surviving Holm correction. A sudden knockout yields the expected zero lead, and a harmless change triggers no alarm. Leads track the length of the transitional phase (Spearman 0.79 over 150 runs). On real transaction ego-networks, the untuned mass channel forewarns staged drift by 27 steps and is the only channel, attributional or structural, that never alarms on a stationary stream. The main limitation is that the mass channel is blind to covariate drift, which breaks the guarantee in every run; the distributional channel detects it and also rescues the rewiring regime, so we report the two channels separately rather than as a union.

items.title: Overtaught, Underlearned: Learner-Centered Distillation from Multi-Agent Discussion
items.description: arXiv:2610.16543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent discussion produces reasoning collaboratively, while deployment still relies on a smaller student that must answer alone. Full-graph distillation transfers such discussions by treating each correct solution as a separate training target, but what teachers provide need not match what the student learns. This mismatch appears in two ways: several correct solutions may amount to the same lesson in the student's representation (over-teaching), while some training questions remain missed after learning (under-learning). We quantify both with rates that are high on discussion graphs. To address them, we introduce FAR (Fold--Attempt--Revisit), a learner-centered distillation procedure that organizes supervision around the student's own state. Before training, FAR folds solutions within each discussion state into representative lessons. After training, the student's own attempts identify missed questions, while poorly represented clusters indicate where folding may have lost useful variation; FAR then writes targeted lessons from retained discussion contexts. Across two students and four reasoning tasks, FAR outperforms full-graph distillation with far fewer training targets and lower under-learning. Further analyses examine the behavior of FAR and the sources of its gains. Overall, the results show that organizing discussion supervision around the student can make distillation both more effective and more efficient.

items.title: Making Language the Low-Rate Code of Vision: Successive Refinement from Words to Pixels
items.description: arXiv:2610.16552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An ordered visual code lets a short prefix stand in for an image, and the training loss decides what that prefix contains. Under pixel reconstruction the first bits go to the directions of highest variance, and we prove that a caption can then be independent of the entire first half of a code that is rate-optimal for pixels at every length. In the rate-distortion sense a caption is therefore not the low-rate code of its image, unless the code is built to make it one. We study that construction and what it costs. We cast captioning and text-to-image generation as successive refinement under a distortion measure that changes along the code, from caption log-loss in the early stages to pixel distortion in the last, so that each stage is compared with its own optimum. Putting words first then costs nothing among the caption stages exactly when the captions form a summarization chain, and it costs the pixels at most the caption uncertainty left in a pixel-optimal reconstruction, which is large for short prefixes and small at full length. We build RUNG, an ordered code whose prefixes are supervised by a summarization ladder of captions and whose full length reconstructs the image; generation extends the code past the prompt and captioning truncates it. With data and capacity held fixed, ordering by language instead of reconstruction raises prefix-caption information 2.9 times and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83, at a measured cost of 2.8 dB PSNR at a quarter of the code and 0.1 dB at full length. RUNG-XL (3.4B) reaches 0.88 GenEval and 87.6 DPG-Bench in 32 network evaluations and 0.91 GenEval when errors are redrawn at the rung where they appear; its coarse and fine captions agree 94.1% of the time, and it edits images without inversion.

items.title: AI Discovery in Combinatorics: From Problems to Solutions and Back to Bigger Problems
items.description: arXiv:2610.16555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce $qt$Bench, a benchmark of 29 open problems in algebraic combinatorics. These problems ask for a simple combinatorial algorithm that explains given polynomial coefficients or identities. To help AI agents search for such algorithms, we provide a scaffold for playing with combinatorial objects, countering cheating attempts, and testing candidate solutions. To explore how far frontier AI systems can go on these problems, we collaborated with OpenAI, whose researchers obtained proposed solutions to several of them. This highlights bigger meta-problems: is AI discovery at scale ethical? How should these results be released? How should proof digestion be organized? We discuss these questions and give our views.

items.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
items.description: arXiv:2610.16558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.

items.title: Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation
items.description: arXiv:2610.16593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.

items.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
items.description: arXiv:2610.16615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.

items.title: Weak Segmentation-Guided GAN for~Realistic Color Edition
items.description: arXiv:2610.16620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Editing the color of images in a realistic way finds many applications such as changing the perception of an image, data augmentation or film post processing. The design of an automatic tool is a complex and long addressed challenge. In particular, two properties are difficult to meet altogether: generating realistic results without artifacts and the possibility to precisely choose the future color. Conventional methods using segmentation and histogram matching maximize the controllability but also introduce a lack of realism or are complex to automate. On the contrary, GANs that specialize in realism are difficult to control. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel GAN architecture leveraging any differentiable segmentation model. We demonstrate the genericness of our framework that presents state of the art results on different use cases. It generates images that look realistic while offering a precise color control.

items.title: LATCH: LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness for Post-Route FPGA Optimisation
items.description: arXiv:2610.16625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-route FPGA timing closure remains expert-dependent and computationally expensive. We present LATCH (LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness), a two-layer framework that separates large language model (LLM) orchestration from deterministic FPGA implementation and evaluation. Across sixteen designs and seven LLMs, a single-iteration study compares three agent control granularities - expert-written recipes, direct EDA operations and LLM-constructed procedures - to ask how much control an agent needs per attempt. Functional-pass rates are 98.2%, 71.4% and 17.9%, respectively; yet direct operations give slightly larger 3.4% median Fmax gains when passing, versus 3.2% for recipes. This exposes a trade-off between execution reliability and timing improvement. Informed by this trade-off, a multi-iteration study fixes the action tier at expert recipes to ask how repeated attempts are best organised, comparing a fitted deterministic heuristic with sequential LLM reasoning, branching exploration and knowledge base-guided exploration within 12 checkpoints per run. Branching raises mean maximum-frequency improvement from 10.5% (sequential) to 16.0%, and the knowledge base to 20.3%, improving 15 of 16 designs. Characterisation across 2,421 recipe attempts profiled their gain and validation rates, showing hard-block re-placement gives the largest cumulative mean gain at 41.4MHz.

items.title: Does a Hosted Decision Model Respect Irrelevant Alternatives? A Pre-Registered Test of Option-Set Dependence in Jev
items.description: arXiv:2610.16655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decision APIs that return a probability for each option are routinely used as if those probabilities were properties of the options themselves. That reading is valid only if the model satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): adding an option that is neither the right answer nor its strongest rival should leave the odds between those two unchanged. We test this in a pre-registered study of jev-1.13.0, a hosted decision model, using 299,463 calls on intent classification (BANKING77, CLINC150) and topic classification (AG News). Every added option moves the log-odds between the gold label and the strongest wrong label: the root-mean-square systematic shift is 0.20-0.52 nats, 1.2 to 3 times the run-to-run variation, even when the added option takes at most 0.1% of the probability mass. The shifts are directional. An option similar to the wrong answer draws probability from it (+0.10 nats toward the gold label). A paraphrase of the wrong answer produces an intermediate pattern: the gold label's probability is almost conserved, but the paraphrase receives only about a third of the wrong answer's share rather than the half that strict substitution implies. The distortion grows steadily with the logarithm of the number of options, reaching about 1 nat at 255 options, and off-domain padding pushes the odds against the gold label. In contrast, questions packed into one call do not interact (bias < 0.001). Scoring each option with an independent yes/no question removes the option-set dependence but picks the right answer 8.7 points less often. Jev sits between two local baselines, an option-independent scorer and a prompt readout. Its probabilities are best read as relative to the option list they were computed over.

items.title: Structural Baselines Matter for Agent Failure Detection and Attribution
items.description: arXiv:2610.16661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An LLM agent using tools can fail silently. It stops before the task is done, raises no error, and answers fluently. Two kinds of monitor address this, one deciding whether a run failed and the other naming the step where failure became unavoidable. Much of the reported performance on both tasks comes from regularities that need no model. Failing runs are longer, and the step labelled decisive is usually the last. A rule that always names the last step is correct $67\%$ to $96\%$ of the time here, without reading the run at all. That ceiling reflects how the labels were written, not how agents break. On failures whose decisive step replay can confirm, it falls to near chance. Reporting gain over that rule therefore changes what a score means. Under that correction, methods tested here gain nothing on give-up failures, while several published systems keep a clear advantage on other splits. For detection, the agent's internal states beat transcript length and text similarity on the agent benchmark, and hold up where the text baseline does not. Precision stays low when failures are rare, so such a monitor should rank runs for review, not replace it.

items.title: Trace-to-Architecture: Capability Bottleneck Diagnosis for Harness Revision
items.description: arXiv:2610.16725v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving an LLM agent requires knowing what to change when it fails. Similar failures can require different fixes, and resolving one problem can expose another. We introduce Trace-to-Architecture (T2A), a framework that uses execution trajectories to determine what to change in an agent's harness and when those changes apply. A development agent diagnoses failures using execution evidence from successful and failed tasks, revises the corresponding harness components, and then checks whether target tasks improve, selected successful tasks remain successful, and the edits are actually triggered. New execution evidence guides subsequent diagnosis and revision. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and AppWorld, T2A achieves the highest aggregate score for all three evaluated task agents, exceeding their respective strongest baselines by 6.2--30.3 points. We also integrate T2A's diagnosis and validation procedures into Meta-Harness, improving the resulting harnesses' mean ScienceWorld score by 21.6 points from the same starting harness.

items.title: Queue-Aware Token Communications: Bridging AI Representation and Wireless Service
items.description: arXiv:2610.16730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models and edge intelligence is transforming wireless networks from data-oriented communication systems into artificial intelligence (AI)-native service platforms. Token communications (TokenCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm that directly transmits task-oriented AI representations. However, existing studies typically assume that generated tokens can be transmitted immediately, overlooking the queueing dynamics arising from the mismatch between token workload generation and time-varying wireless service capability. To address this limitation, we introduce Queue-Aware TokenCom, which explicitly incorporates token queues into the AI service pipeline. We present an end-to-end architecture integrating AI representation generation, token workload management, wireless transmission, and downstream task inference. We then discuss two key design directions: budget-aware token representation optimization and queue-aware token service optimization, with the token budget serving as a critical interface between AI performance and communication efficiency. Moreover, we investigate fixed and adaptive token budget strategies to characterize the fundamental tradeoff between AI performance and communication efficiency in dynamic wireless environments. Finally, we outline research directions toward closed-loop, task-aware, and scalable TokenCom systems.

items.title: Separating Prompt Harmfulness from Interaction Safety via Partial Generation
items.description: arXiv:2610.16761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based information systems need safety guardrails. Most guardrails classify the prompt alone. If the prompt looks harmful, the system rejects it before any answer is generated. This is costly. Many rejected prompts would have received a safe response. Users lose help they should have received from the information system. This cost grows as conversational and generative search becomes common. Prompt-level labels treat harm as a property of the query. But harm depends on what the model actually writes. Existing input-output guards do look at responses. But they judge a finished response, so the decision comes after full generation. However, we observe that safety of model interaction with the input prompt can be inferred early with only partial output. So the system can start generating, watch the partial response, and stop only if it turns harmful. We test this idea in three steps. First, we build a dataset of 41,944 prompt-response pairs with seven open weights LLMs from three families: Llama, Gemma, and Qwen. Second, we show that prompt harmfulness and interaction safety differ. Prompt labels and response labels agree on only 50.46\% of items (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.06). Of the prompts that make any model respond harmfully, only 3.5\% do so for all seven LLMs. Third, we show that partial responses carry most of the signal. Fine-tuned classifiers predict response-level harm well (best AUPRC 0.885, F1 0.807). About one third of the response tokens recover almost full-response AUPRC.

items.title: Geospatial Vector Geometry as a Native Spatial Modality for Vision-Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.16769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geospatial reasoning links VLMs to real-world action and decision making. Reliable reasoning requires accurate spatial information and effective spatial representations. However, current VLMs obtain this information mainly from language and vision. At larger geographic scales, limited visual observations make it difficult to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. This leads to a bottleneck for VLM spatial perception and reasoning. This paper proposes that geospatial vector geometry can become a native spatial modality within a VLM and introduces GeoVec-VLM. First, we develop a structured geometry representation that preserves the spatial structure and arrangement of vector objects, building an explicit spatial basis. Second, we introduce a geometry interaction strategy that brings this basis into multimodal computation, where it interacts with visual content and language references according to the queried spatial relations. Together, these designs allow perception and reasoning to operate on shared geometric references. Across five spatial reasoning tasks, GeoVec-VLM improves mean accuracy by about 11\% relative to the strongest baseline, maintains its gains under geographic transfer, and shows greater geometric consistency. Our results show that geospatial vector geometry offers a promising internal spatial basis for VLM spatial reasoning. https://github.com/TXFR/GeoVector-VLM

items.title: Game-Creation-Agents: Autonomous Game Production
items.description: arXiv:2610.16776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Game-Creation-Agents (GCA) turns a natural-language request into a runnable Phaser 4 browser game. The pipeline first builds a multimodal game design document that couples mechanics and scene contracts to grounded visual references. It then projects that document into a runtime scaffold, machine-readable contracts, and deterministic tests. Eight specialized agents next carry out production: scenes are implemented serially, assets are produced in parallel, and one reduced manifest joins the two branches into a single build. Build-linked real-UI checks and a code-blind critic then verify that build and decide whether the game may ship. Each blocker returns to the agent that owns the affected artifact for a bounded repair, and the game is released once all the gates pass. We evaluate finished games separately, through their rendered interfaces alone, over prompt-matched tasks run under a common protocol. GCA achieves stronger requirement satisfaction, core mechanics, content depth, and functional visuals than a comparable open pipeline. In a side-by-side human study, raters also score GCA's games higher on every dimension and prefer them overall.

items.title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints
items.description: arXiv:2610.16782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

items.title: Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization
items.description: arXiv:2610.16838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As language-model agents write code, move money and change records on behalf of users, deciding whether an action is authorized has become a central safety problem. Guardrails are often placed in front of these actions, yet few evaluations ask whether their decisions follow authorization: blocking unauthorized actions while still allowing the same actions under valid permission. We introduce \bench{}, a benchmark that contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation in its language track. It combines expert-annotated natural-language scenarios with executed and verified operations, plus externally sourced native-policy requests. \bench{} checks each decision for correctness, usability and resulting effect, and tracks each request across guardrail changes. Our experiments show that many blocked operations stem from failed reviews, not correct denials. Repairing the output format restores usable decisions but changes which authorized requests are honored, and adding a second reviewer removes some errors while rejecting valid authorization. Guardrails should therefore be evaluated on both the unauthorized actions they stop and the authorized actions they let through.

items.title: CLIVO: Differentiable Cluster-Based Instruction Mixing with Learned Validation Objectives
items.description: arXiv:2610.16876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Target-aware multimodal instruction selection requires useful examples and an appropriate balance of supervision. Sample-level rankings can overrepresent similar content without optimizing this balance; group-level methods face coarse units, predefined set-level validation signals, and costly or inaccurate mixture search. We propose CLIVO, a target-aware framework connecting fine-grained semantic allocation, automatically learned validation objectives, and differentiable mixture search. Specifically, semantic clusters provide independently adjustable shares at the hundred-cluster scale. Correlations between per-example merged-proxy losses and real probe performance identify target-relevant validation examples; learned nonnegative weights combine their losses into an objective. A single backward pass through the merged proxy supplies gradients for all shares, avoiding an additional mixture-response regression model. Selecting 100K instructions from an 8M pool, CLIVO attains 97.2% of the full-data four-target average score with only 1.25% of the data. It improves on the strongest evaluated selection baseline by 1.16 points using random within-cluster sampling; combining learned quotas with sample ranking increases this advantage to 1.55 points. Analyses show that finer units benefit most targets, short-trained experts preserve mixture responses, sample weighting retains useful validation information, and direct search consistently reduces the learned objective. CLIVO also supports interpretable allocation, modular selection, and reuse across targets and granularities.

items.title: Acceptable Misalignment
items.description: arXiv:2610.16881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There is a specific challenge designers face in developing autonomous robots capable of open-ended learning. This challenge is how one can develop such systems in an ethically sound way when there are many unknowns during design time about their manner of deployment, what they can and will learn, and how these systems will act on the basis of what they have learned. One response to this challenge is to align, as far as possible, the activities and goals of autonomous robots with human values, raising the question of how to make this alignment possible, a question known as the value alignment problem. We argue that the value alignment problem faces a number of challenges that show that full alignment is both theoretically and practically impossible, meaning that misalignment incidents will keep occurring. This undermines current alignment approaches, as the attempt to maximize alignment cannot properly deal with the possibility that the risk of misalignment that remains after alignment methods have been implemented might still be unacceptable to society. To overcome this difficulty, we argue that a shift in perspective is required from a focus on the maximization of alignment to the conditions under which misalignment incidents become acceptable. In this paper, we explore what this shift in perspective entails. We introduce the concept of acceptable misalignment, formulate normative requirements for alignment mechanisms aimed at bringing misalignment incidents to an acceptable level, and we conclude by presenting a new methodological framework that consists of alignment mechanisms that can meet these requirements.

items.title: Transparency as Answerability: Role-Dependent Information Flow Modeling
items.description: arXiv:2610.16887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transparency in AI-supported decision systems is widely required but poorly defined. Existing approaches treat transparency as a property of systems or components, producing characteristic failures: assessments that do not transfer across organizational boundaries, stakeholder questions that cannot be formulated within the available frame of analysis, and component-level findings that say nothing about system-level behavior. We propose treating transparency as a relation: a system is transparent to a stakeholder to the degree that their legitimate questions are answerable from its structure. We formalize this using information flow networks, in which transparency questions are expressed in terms of network structure and answerability is the condition that the system settles them. The framework supports three dimensions of analysis: structural answerability from the network alone, compositional answerability across organizational boundaries for deployed systems, and role-dependent answerability given a stakeholder's accessible sub-network. We demonstrate the framework on a real pre-integration assessment of an AI recruitment tool in a public sector municipality. The assessment uses participatory design and interviews to model the decision system structure. We show how structural and role-dependent transparency questions can be formally stated and analyzed across the Provider and Deployer boundary where the AI system is composed together with the deployer's decision process.

items.title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
items.description: arXiv:2610.16895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

items.title: Neural Bayesian Networks for Modular and Scalable Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
items.description: arXiv:2610.16902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian Networks (BNs) are established tools for letting agents reason under uncertainty in sequential decision-making. They split a joint distribution into local conditional mechanisms arranged on a directed acyclic graph, which makes them modular, interpretable, and ready to perform probabilistic inference. Their classical formulation, however, has limitations in both expressiveness and scale: each conditional is usually stored as a table or a linear-Gaussian form, and inference evaluates the graph one node and one query at a time. In this paper we introduce Neural Bayesian Networks (NBNs), in which each conditional is a differentiable, tensor-valued mechanism, while the graph and its factorization are unchanged. NBNs retain the modularity and local mechanisms of BNs, can represent any learnable conditional distribution, and run natively on GPUs. We also release NBN, a PyTorch-based library for learning and inference in NBNs, together with a public benchmark. Our evaluation shows gains in both expressiveness and scale: NBNs fit distributions that classical BN libraries struggle to represent, and on large networks and large batches of queries they run two orders of magnitude faster thanks to GPU parallelization. NBN is available at https://github.com/Giovannibriglia/NeuralBayesianNetworks.

items.title: Audit tools of the trade: Automated Auditor Elicitation Can Be Sensitive to the Context the Auditor Is Given
items.description: arXiv:2610.16911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does providing additional context to automated AI auditors improve their effectiveness? Using the Petri tool to audit LLM coding agents, we test the impact of providing two types of resources (an external codebase and benchmark transcripts) to LLM auditors, across four auditor-target LLM pairs and three behaviours (harmful compliance, reward hacking, sycophancy). (1) External codebase: We provide the auditor LLM with a fixed, external open source codebase, which prior work finds improves the realism of synthetic audits. Providing this resource suppresses reward hacking in both auditor-target pairs whose baseline rate is above the floor (4.8 to 1.3 and 3.9 to 1.8 on Petri's default 1-10 scale); the remaining two pairs sit at the floor throughout. The suppression recurs in three of four pairs under a different scenario and resource bundle. (2) External benchmark transcripts: We provide the auditor with transcripts of the target's performance on benchmarks measuring similar behaviours, intended to inform the auditor about the target's behavioural patterns. Providing this resource raises reward hacking scores in all four pairs (from 1.7 to 6.1 in one case). However, subsequent experiments show that supplying only the related benchmark's abstract, without transcripts, also increases reward hacking, and the effect is absent under a different framing of the same behaviour. Overall, we find no consistent effect of either resource outside reward hacking, but we find substantial variability in judge-scored behaviour across conditions. Our results underscore the importance of careful piloting with tools such as Petri, as the measured rate of target behaviour is highly sensitive to configuration decisions. We hope our results inspire more research into the reliability and robustness of automated alignment auditing.

items.title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
items.description: arXiv:2610.16916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.

items.title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
items.description: arXiv:2610.16927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short-video search requires compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. The challenge is to decide when personalization is warranted and generate a reformulation that preserves the user's immediate information need. A rewriter optimized for fluency or engagement may still introduce unsupported details and redirect the search toward a different intent. Existing methods often underutilize users' actual reformulations and behavioral traces, relying instead on synthetic reasoning and indirect behavioral rewards that may produce more engaging candidates but cause intent drift. To build an effective rewriter that remains faithful to user intent, we propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair assigns real user behavioral signals to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual human reformulations from search sessions, then apply multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification to filter unsupported transitions without extensive manual annotation. During training, we begin with a supervised curriculum that progressively builds rewriting capabilities from large-scale human personalized query demonstrations, and then use direct preference optimization to align with users' subsequent consumption. In the final on-policy optimization stage, we construct a strict verification reward based on actual human reformulations to further boost performance with group relative policy optimization. Further analysis shows that auxiliary rewards can activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity. Online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search shows a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate (VV>10s) and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate.

items.title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
items.description: arXiv:2610.16975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

items.title: PRAISE: A Reproducible Workflow for Non-Programmer Scientists to Implement Published AI Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.16980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step.
